questions.topic: Period of a mass-spring oscillator
questions.learningObjective: compute the period of a mass oscillating on an ideal spring
questions.stem: A 2.0 kg mass is attached to an ideal spring of stiffness 200 N/m on a frictionless surface. What is the period of the resulting oscillation in seconds?
questions.explanation: The period is 2 pi times the square root of m over k, so the ratio is 2.0 over 200 = 0.010 s^2, its square root is 0.100 s, and 2 pi times that is 0.6283 s. The units confirm the arrangement, because k over m = 100 s^-2 has the square root of a frequency while m over k has the square root of a time. Rewriting the answer as the reciprocal of the quarter-period frequency, 2 pi over 21.2 s^-1, gives the same 0.6283 s.
questions.hint: Use T = 2 pi times the square root of m divided by k, and check that the result carries units of seconds.

questions.topic: Small-angle period of a pendulum

questions.stem: A simple pendulum of length 0.75 m is set swinging through a small angle on a planet where g = 9.8 m/s^2. What is its period in seconds?

questions.hint: Use T = 2 pi times the square root of L divided by g, valid while the swing angle stays small.

questions.learningObjective: state the condition that defines simple harmonic motion
questions.stem: A system is said to be in simple harmonic motion when its acceleration obeys a particular rule. Which statement gives that rule correctly?

The acceleration is proportional to the displacement and points the same way as it

options.text: The acceleration is constant, because a steady force gives a steady acceleration

options.misconception: confuses the restoring condition with a speed-proportional damping force

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why a small-angle pendulum period ignores amplitude
questions.learningObjective: explain why the small-angle pendulum period does not depend on amplitude
questions.stem: Using the restoring torque mgL sin theta, explain why the period of a pendulum does not depend on how far it is swung as long as the angle stays small.

answer.exemplar: The restoring torque on a pendulum of length L is mgL sin theta, and for a small angle sin theta is very nearly theta itself, so the equation of motion becomes mL squared times the angular acceleration equals minus mgL theta. Dividing through by the moment of inertia mL squared leaves angular acceleration equal to minus g over L times theta, a linear restoring law identical in form to a spring's, and a linear restoring law has solutions whose timing depends only on the constants in the equation. Because theta never appears, the size of the swing drops out and the period is 2 pi times the square root of L over g, the same for a 5 degree and a 10 degree release. The mass cancels for the same reason, since a heavier bob needs proportionally more torque to the same acceleration. The approximation is the only caveat: at 60 degrees sin theta is 0.866 where theta in radians is 1.047, the restoring torque is weaker per radian, and the true period runs about 7 per cent longer than the small-angle formula.

questions.explanation: A complete answer derives the linear restoring law from mgL sin theta, identifies the linear equation as the reason the timing is amplitude-free, notes that the mass cancels, and explains that the small-angle condition is what licenses sin theta equal to theta, with the large-angle error running to a longer period.
questions.hint: Reduce the restoring torque to a linear one, then ask what a linear restoring law does to the timing.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why a standing wave carries energy nowhere
questions.learningObjective: explain why a standing wave transports no net energy along a string
questions.stem: Two identical wave trains run along a string in opposite directions at the same speed, producing a standing wave. Explain why no energy is carried along the string even though the string itself is moving.

answer.exemplar: Energy transport requires a velocity times a positive energy density, and in a standing wave the two trains carry equal amounts in opposite directions, so the two contributions cancel at every point. The string does move, but the motion is a local oscillation about a fixed node or antinode rather than a travelling pattern, so the velocity of each piece of string reverses every half cycle while the energy density stays non-negative throughout. A travelling wave has the property that the string's velocity and its slope always have the same sign, which is exactly the condition for energy to flow in one direction, and a standing wave has no such sign agreement. The individual trains do carry energy, and each exists on its own, but where they overlap the pattern is stationary and the net flux is zero, which is why a bowed string can sound a note without the energy running along it.

questions.explanation: A full answer explains that the two equal and opposite travelling components give equal and opposite energy fluxes which cancel, notes that the local motion is an oscillation about a fixed point rather than a travelling pattern, and can cite the velocity-slope sign condition for energy flow.
questions.hint: Energy flows when a moving medium carries energy along; ask which way the medium is moving.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Doppler formula for a moving source
questions.learningObjective: explain why the moving-source and moving-observer cases differ
questions.stem: Explain why the Doppler shift for a moving source and for a moving observer take different forms, and what goes wrong if the two are swapped.

answer.exemplar: The speed of sound in the medium is fixed by the medium, so a moving source does not change the speed of the waves it emits but instead changes the spacing between them: while it advances by v_s times the period, it leaves a wavelength shortened to (v - v_s) over f, and the stationary listener therefore receives f times v over (v - v_s). A moving observer changes no spacing at all, since the source's wavefronts are already formed, and it simply meets them at the relative speed v + v_o, giving f times (v + v_o) over v. Swapping the two therefore puts the moving speed on the wrong side of the wrong fraction, and although the two agree when the shift is small enough for either form to be used, they diverge noticeably at 30 m/s in air: a 600 Hz tone heard by an approaching listener is 653 Hz, while the same 600 Hz heard by a stationary listener from an approaching source is 658 Hz. The results are close, which is exactly why the misapplied form is hard to catch by eye, and the physical distinction between compressing a wavelength and increasing the arrival rate is what separates them.

questions.explanation: A full answer derives the moving-source form from a shortened wavelength and the moving-observer form from an increased rate of arrival, then shows the two give different numbers for the same speeds and explains that the compressed wavelength versus faster arrival is the real distinction.
questions.hint: Ask whether the moving body is changing the wavefront spacing or the rate at which wavefronts are met.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: A claim that superposition rules out
questions.learningObjective: identify a wave claim that the superposition principle contradicts
questions.stem: A colleague claims that two sound waves meeting in the same region of air pass through one another completely unaffected, so a listener can never detect that they overlapped. Explain why the superposition principle makes that claim untenable.

answer.exemplar: Superposition says only that the displacement of overlapping waves adds, which is precisely what makes the claim untenable: where the two add in step the amplitude is doubled and where they oppose it is cut down, and both states last for a measurable time. Beats are the audible case, since a listener reports a pulsing at the difference of two nearby frequencies that no single source ever produced, and the same addition gives the quiet points of an interference pattern. The medium's total displacement is genuinely the sum at every instant, so nothing is destroyed, but the sum is not the same as each part taken alone, and the claim survives only by confusing additivity with immunity. It also contradicts the standing wave, where the two trains combine into a pattern that neither could form alone.

questions.explanation: A complete answer states that the displacement in an overlap is the sum of the two waves, that this sum is measurably different from either part alone, gives beats or an interference pattern as the audible evidence, and concludes that additivity is not the same as the waves being unaffected by one another.
questions.hint: If the waves really were unaffected, the sum would carry no information that neither part had.
